items.log_text: Four-shaft loom reassembled in the lower corridor. Heddle frames are warped wire in a wood rail — crude but the eyes are even enough. Plain weave tie-up first; no time for complexity. Warp of hemp two-ply, sixty centimetres wide.

Switched to two-two twill on the same threading. Tied treadles three and four together for the advancing diagonal. Cloth came off the loom with a surface sheen the plain weave lacked. Stronger in the warp direction under load.

Broken twill interrupts the diagonal — reversed the sequence at the treadle every eight picks. Surface pattern is less regular but the structure locks in both directions. Useful for anything that needs to resist puncture.

Pine frame, eight shafts — the most complex tie-up so far. Point threading means the diagonal reverses at the centre. Threading took most of a morning. First cloth off shows a chevron ridge. We have not made anything this fine before.

Honeycomb block tie-up. Warp floats form a raised cell pattern — the air trapped inside gives real insulating bulk. Slower to weave: five picks per cell, each block eight ends wide. Worth the time for blanket weight.

Second warp, same threading. Linen two-ply at tighter sett: seventy-two ends per ten centimetres. Takes longer to beat down but the resulting cloth is nearly windproof. Cut into panels for the shelter door seal.

Satinette tie-up — warp-float dominant, seven-shaft cycle. The surface is almost smooth. Very slow; broke two heddle wires in the tighter shafts. The cloth catches light differently. First time anyone has commented on what we made as a thing, not just a thing we needed.
